strengths: The framework addresses a useful need: generating related graphs with persistent community identities and configurable structural and feature distributions for inductive evaluation.
The universe–family–instance organization is intuitive, and coupling community identities to features, connectivity patterns, and degree profiles offers useful experimental flexibility.

The empirical study covers nine architectures, multiple distribution shifts, and two prediction tasks. Architecture-specific hyperparameter searches, three dataset seeds, and extensive implementation appendices are positive aspects.

Validation across 100 randomized families provides evidence that several generation parameters influence the intended properties, while the benchmarking results suggest interesting architecture-dependent sensitivities.
weaknesses: The novelty and positioning are overstated. Independent sampling does not fundamentally prevent inductive evaluation: standard SBMs can generate multiple graphs sharing block parameters, label identities, and feature distributions. Standard DC-SBMs also need not have uniform block probabilities. The paper needs a comparison against this straightforward shared-parameter construction and ablations establishing the additional value of persistent structural and degree signatures. Claims of the first systematic inductive evaluation are not adequately substantiated.

The mathematical calibration contains substantive errors. Equation (18) uses n² when averaging a k-by-k block matrix requires k². Appendix B incorrectly simplifies the within-community expected edge count: even without clipping, mean-one degree factors give Prr[(nr)² − sum_i(theta_i²)]/2, rather than Prr nr(nr−1)/2 in general. Appendix D then uses global rather than per-community normalization, further invalidating the stated calibration guarantees. These issues require corrected derivations and verification against the implementation.

Precise control of homophily and degree is not established. Block scaling omits finite community-size weighting; heterogeneous degree factors, clipping, and connectivity repair subsequently change the target quantities. Connectivity alone makes average degree below 2(n−1)/n impossible, despite the experimental range starting at 1. Strong Pearson correlations demonstrate responsiveness, not agreement with targets. Absolute calibration errors, clipping frequencies, and repair-induced changes should be reported across operating regimes.

The central inductive–transductive comparison is heavily confounded. Table 4 compares 1,000 graphs with 50–200 nodes and 4–6 participating communities against one 1,000-node graph containing all 10 communities, while also changing degree separation, power-law settings, and parameter variability. Training-label budgets differ substantially. Consequently, ranking changes cannot be attributed specifically to the evaluation paradigm, and explanations involving GIN memorization or NSD's generalization bias remain speculative.

Some validation and evaluation choices weaken the conclusions. The structural-signal classifier uses ground-truth neighbor-community counts, making it an oracle diagnostic rather than evidence that equivalent information is accessible to the benchmarked models. Triangle-counting results lack trivial constant/count-statistic baselines and target-distribution summaries. Dividing MAE by graph size can make size-generalization results appear better as graphs grow, so raw errors and suitable normalized baselines are needed before concluding that models maintain counting performance.

The scalability claim is unsupported by the reported measurements. Table 1 shows generation time increasing from 0.020 to 1.070 seconds for a tenfold increase in node count, approximately a 53-fold increase, contrary to the stated linear scaling across graph sizes. The described all-pairs edge sampling also requires quadratic work. Two graph sizes and no memory measurements do not establish suitability for large-scale foundation-model data generation.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Section 5.3 specifies homophily shifts of ±0.1 and node-count shifts, whereas Figure 3B reports homophily shifts of ±0.30 and feature-variance shifts of ±0.20. Training duration, stopping criteria, and triangle-task model selection are insufficiently specified, and scripts/configurations are deferred until acceptance. These discrepancies make the experiments difficult to reconstruct and the mathematical errors difficult to distinguish from implementation errors.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: controlled evaluation of generalization across graphs with persistent community identities and tunable structural and feature distributions.
The universe–family–graph organization provides an understandable framework for constructing related datasets and distribution shifts.
The evaluation covers nine architectures, two tasks, three dataset seeds, and architecture-specific hyperparameter searches. The randomized generator validation is also a worthwhile effort.
weaknesses: The novelty argument is overstated. Independently sampling graphs does not inherently prevent inductive evaluation: shared SBM parameters and feature distributions can define consistent training and test graphs. Standard SBMs also allow heterogeneous block probabilities. The paper needs a comparison against this straightforward shared-parameter baseline and ablations establishing the benefit of its additional hierarchy and degree coupling.

The claimed control of graph properties is not established mathematically. Appendix C, Eq. (18), uses n² when averaging a k×k block matrix, where k² would be required for the stated mean-entry constraint. Appendix B incorrectly simplifies within-community expected edge counts: mean-one normalization gives a factor n_r² − Σ_i θ_i², not n_r(n_r−1), even without clipping. These errors undermine the derivation and require clarification against the implementation.

Global degree normalization, probability clipping, and connectivity repair can all alter target homophily and average degree. Some advertised settings are incompatible with connectivity: a connected n-node graph has average degree at least 2(n−1)/n, whereas experiments sample targets as low as 1. Correlations between requested and observed properties do not demonstrate calibration; absolute errors and parameter-interaction analyses are needed.

The central inductive-versus-transductive comparison is substantially confounded. Table 4 changes graph size (50–200 versus 1,000 nodes), communities per graph (4–6 versus 10), training-data volume, degree separation, and power-law exponent distributions. Consequently, ranking changes cannot confidently be attributed to the evaluation paradigm, and explanations involving memorization or architectural generalization biases remain speculative.

Triangle-counting size generalization is inadequately validated. Figure 4 reports MAE divided by graph size without raw errors, target distributions, or constant and simple statistical baselines. At fixed expected degree, triangle counts need not grow proportionally with node count, so this normalization can make larger-graph performance appear better without improved prediction. The conclusion that models effectively solve and generalize the task is therefore insufficiently supported.

The scalability claim conflicts with the reported measurements: increasing graph size from 100 to 1,000 nodes increases generation time from 0.020 to 1.070 seconds, approximately 54-fold. This does not demonstrate linear scaling in graph size, and the described pairwise edge sampling is quadratic.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code and configurations are deferred until acceptance, and the shift protocol is inconsistent between Section 5.3 (±0.1 homophily and ±200 nodes) and Figure 3 (±0.30 homophily and ±0.20 cluster variance). These discrepancies are material for reproducing the robustness findings.

strengths: Addresses a useful benchmarking need: generating related graphs with persistent community identities enables controlled studies of generalization to unseen graphs.

The universe–family–instance organization is intuitive, with configurable feature, structural, and degree signals. The proposed interactive interface and TopoBench integration could make the framework practically useful.
Experiments cover nine architectures, two tasks, several distribution shifts, and three dataset seeds, with model-specific hyperparameter searches and reported variability.
Validation across 100 randomized families provides useful evidence of parameter responsiveness, and the observed dependence of robustness on the training regime merits further investigation.
weaknesses: The central inductive–transductive comparison is substantially confounded. Table 4 compares 1,000 graphs with 50–200 nodes and 4–6 participating communities against one 1,000-node graph containing all 10 communities, while also changing degree separation and power-law parameters. Training-label budgets differ greatly. Consequently, ranking changes do not isolate the evaluation paradigm, and explanations involving GIN memorization or superior inductive architectural biases are unsupported.

The generator's calibration derivation contains substantive errors. Equation (18) uses n² when scaling the mean of a k×k matrix, which would require k² under its stated criterion. Appendix B incorrectly simplifies the within-community degree-factor sum: under mean-one normalization it is n_r² minus the sum of squared degree factors, not generally n_r(n_r−1). These discrepancies require correction and verification against the implementation.

Claims of precise property control exceed the evidence. Global degree-factor normalization, probability clipping, and connectivity repair can systematically change degree and homophily. Connectivity alone makes average degree below 2(n−1)/n impossible, although the benchmark samples targets from [1,5]. Pearson correlations demonstrate responsiveness, not calibration; target-versus-realized errors and intervention ablations are needed.

Novelty is overstated by repeatedly claiming that independent graph generation or DC-SBMs fundamentally prevent inductive evaluation. Repeated sampling with shared block parameters and feature centroids already permits related graph families. The paper needs a clearer distinction from this straightforward baseline and ablations demonstrating the added value of its hierarchy and community–degree coupling.

The scalability claim is unsupported. Table 1 reports a runtime increase from 0.020 to 1.070 seconds for a tenfold increase in nodes, contradicting the stated linear scaling across graph sizes. Explicit pairwise edge sampling is quadratic, and two graph sizes up to 1,000 nodes provide insufficient evidence for foundation-model-scale generation.

Triangle-counting conclusions need stronger controls. MAE divided by graph size can obscure size-dependent target difficulty; raw errors, target statistics, and simple constant or size-based predictors are missing. The claim that NSD maintains performance on larger graphs also needs qualification because it runs out of memory at the largest tested size.

Reproducibility and experimental reporting remain incomplete. Code and configurations are deferred until acceptance, and the supplied manuscript has blank demo links. Section 5.3 describes ±0.1 homophily shifts, whereas Figure 3 shows ±0.30; its description also differs from the plotted feature-noise shifts. These inconsistencies obstruct verification of the reported robustness results.

strengths: Addresses a relevant benchmarking need: generating related graphs with persistent community identities permits controlled evaluation on unseen graphs and under distribution shifts.
The universe–family–instance organization is interpretable and combines structural, degree, and feature signals in a useful experimental framework.

The empirical study covers multiple architecture families, non-message-passing baselines, heterophily-specialized models, two prediction tasks, and five real datasets. Architecture-specific hyperparameter searches and three data seeds are positive features.

Real-data ranking correlations provide encouraging preliminary evidence of utility. The appendices also explicitly acknowledge limitations of community-based generation and distinguish potential foundation-model applications from demonstrated capabilities.
weaknesses: The novelty argument overstates limitations of prior generators. Independent sampling from an SBM/DC-SBM does not inherently prevent inductive evaluation: shared block parameters, label identities, and feature distributions can be retained across samples. The paper needs a matched multi-graph baseline with shared parameters, plus ablations of persistent features, structural propensities, and degree coupling, to establish the benefit of its particular hierarchy.

The mathematical specification does not support the claimed precise parameter control. Equation (21) uses n² to normalize a k-by-k matrix; its stated mean-entry constraint requires k². Appendix C incorrectly simplifies within-community expected edges to Prr·nr(nr−1)/2: even without clipping, the expression under mean-one normalization is Prr·(nr²−Σi θi²)/2. Appendix F then uses global rather than per-community normalization. These discrepancies require correction and reconciliation with the implementation.

Clipping, unequal community degree factors, finite community sizes, and connectivity repair can systematically change both degree and homophily. Some advertised settings are incompatible with connectivity: connected n-node graphs require average degree at least 2(n−1)/n, whereas experiments request degrees down to 1. High Pearson correlations in the validation study do not establish calibration; quantitative target-versus-realized errors and feasibility handling are needed.

The central inductive-versus-transductive comparison is substantially confounded. Table 6 compares 1,000 graphs of 50–200 nodes against one 1,000-node graph, while also changing participating community counts, degree-separation settings, and power-law exponents. Training-label budgets differ greatly. Consequently, ranking changes cannot be attributed specifically to inductive generalization, and explanations involving GIN memorization or architectural generalization biases remain speculative.

The real-world proxy experiment has an inadequately matched comparator. GraphUniverse uses small graph families, while GraphWorld uses a single 1,000-node graph with different community counts. Correlations involve only six graph-aware models after baseline exclusion; Figure 10 reports p=0.072 for two datasets and p=0.266 for IMDB-MULTI, where GraphWorld actually has higher Spearman correlation (0.60 versus 0.54). These results are promising but insufficient for claims of consistently superior, reliable architecture selection.

The linear-scaling claim contradicts both the pairwise generation procedure and Table 1: doubling graph size from 500 to 1,000 increases runtime from 0.349 to 1.309 seconds, approximately 3.75-fold. Measurements only through 1,000 nodes do not substantiate broader scalability claims.

Reporting inconsistencies impede reproducibility. Section 5.3 specifies homophily shifts of ±0.1, whereas Figure 3 uses ±0.30 and additionally reports feature-noise shifts. Figures 10 and 11 appear duplicated despite claiming different model sets. Training duration, stopping criteria, and task-specific model-selection details are insufficiently specified. Together with the methodological issues above, these weaknesses leave the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The problem is relevant: generating graph families with persistent community identities provides a useful setting for studying generalization to unseen graphs and controlled distribution shifts.

The framework combines structural, degree, and feature controls in an interpretable hierarchy. The parameter-validation study covers 3,000 graphs, and the benchmarking includes diverse architectures, hyperparameter searches, three data seeds, and additional heterophily-focused models.

The real-data comparison is a useful attempt to establish practical relevance. Excluding weak non-message-passing baselines from the correlation analysis is particularly appropriate, and Appendix D acknowledges limitations of community-based generation.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated and insufficiently isolated. Independent graph sampling does not inherently prevent inductive evaluation: an SBM/DC-SBM can generate multiple graphs with shared block parameters, labels, and feature distributions. Standard SBMs also permit heterogeneous block probabilities. The paper needs a direct comparison against this straightforward shared-parameter baseline and ablations separating the benefits of persistent features, structural propensities, and degree coupling.

The claimed probability calibration has substantive mathematical problems. In Appendix E, Eq. (21) uses n² when normalizing the mean of a k-by-k block matrix; the stated mean constraint would require k². Moreover, block sizes, excluded self-loops, community-dependent degree factors, and clipping affect expected degree and homophily. Appendix C incorrectly simplifies the within-community degree-factor sum to n_r(n_r−1); under mean-one normalization it is n_r²−sum_i θ_i². These issues undermine the asserted exact control unless corrected and reconciled with the implementation.

Validation establishes responsiveness rather than calibration. Strong parameter–output correlations do not establish that requested values are achieved. Connectivity correction further changes the distribution: connected n-node graphs require average degree at least 2(n−1)/n, yet default degree targets extend down to 1. Target-versus-realized errors, infeasible-parameter handling, and correction/clipping ablations are needed.

The inductive–transductive comparison is heavily confounded. Table 6 compares 1,000 graphs of 50–200 nodes against one 1,000-node graph, with different numbers of participating communities, degree-separation settings, and power-law parameters. Training-label budgets also differ substantially. Consequently, ranking changes cannot be attributed specifically to inductive generalization, and explanations involving memorization or architectural biases are not established.

Real-world predictive validity remains preliminary. The GraphWorld comparison changes graph size, community counts, parameter variability, and evaluation protocol simultaneously (Appendix K), so it does not isolate the proposed hierarchy. Synthetic node classification is compared with different real graph-level tasks. Among six graph-aware architectures, three of five GraphUniverse rank correlations have p-values above 0.05, and GraphWorld has a higher rank correlation on IMDB-MULTI. These results are encouraging but insufficient for claims of reliable architecture selection.

The scalability claim contradicts the reported measurements. Increasing graph size from 500 to 1,000 nodes increases generation time from 0.349 to 1.309 seconds, approximately 3.75-fold, consistent with the described all-pairs edge sampling rather than linear scaling. Testing only up to 1,000 nodes does not substantiate large-scale generation claims.

Experimental reporting contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 5.3 specifies homophily shifts of ±0.1, whereas Figure 3 shows ±0.30. Figure 11 claims to include the non-message-passing baselines but displays the same six graph-aware models and correlations as Figure 10. Such discrepancies weaken confidence in reproducibility and interpretation.

strengths: The universe–family–instance hierarchy is a useful framework for generating graphs with shared community identities and studying controlled distribution shifts.
The evaluation covers diverse architectures, heterophily-specialized models, two prediction tasks, and five real-world datasets, with hyperparameter searches and three data seeds.
Real-world ranking correlations provide encouraging preliminary evidence of practical relevance; excluding non-message-passing baselines is a sensible robustness check.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and explicitly discusses limitations of community-based graph generation.
weaknesses: The claimed precise control of graph properties has unresolved mathematical problems. Equation (21) uses n² to normalize a k×k matrix; matching its mean would require k². Appendix C incorrectly simplifies the within-community degree-factor sum: mean-one normalization gives n_r² − sum_i θ_i², not n_r(n_r−1). Global normalization, probability clipping, and connectivity correction introduce further systematic deviations. Parameter correlations do not establish calibration accuracy.

The main inductive-versus-transductive comparison is substantially confounded. Table 6 changes graph size, total training examples, communities per graph, degree separation, and power-law exponent alongside the evaluation protocol. Consequently, ranking changes cannot be attributed specifically to inductive generalization, and explanations involving memorization or architectural biases remain speculative.

Novelty is overstated. Independently sampled graphs do not inherently prevent inductive evaluation: shared block parameters and feature distributions can support consistent labels across samples. A matched multi-graph DC-SBM baseline and ablations of shared centroids, structural propensities, and degree coupling are needed to establish the contribution beyond organizing existing generative components.

Real-world proxy validation is promising but insufficiently controlled. GraphUniverse and GraphWorld equivalents differ in graph size, community count, training-data volume, and parameter variability. Correlations involve only six graph-aware models; three of five reported Spearman correlations have p-values above 0.05, and GraphUniverse is slightly worse on IMDB-MULTI. This evidence does not establish reliable architecture selection or isolate the benefit of persistent semantics.

The linear-scaling claim contradicts Table 1: increasing graph size from 500 to 1,000 nodes increases generation time from 0.349 to 1.309 seconds, approximately quadratic behavior and consistent with pairwise edge sampling. Experiments stop at 1,000 nodes, leaving large-scale scalability unsupported.

The triangle-counting conclusions lack controls for shortcuts through graph size, degree, or density. Simple structural-statistic predictors, explicit pooling ablations, and fuller raw-error reporting are needed before concluding that some architectures learn transferable counting while traditional MPNNs overfit graph size.

Experimental reporting contains material inconsistencies: Section 5.3 specifies homophily shifts of ±0.1 whereas Figure 3 uses ±0.3; Figure 11 claims to include non-message-passing baselines but displays the same six graph-aware models. These discrepancies weaken reproducibility and confidence in the reported analyses.
